---
title: "Proximal-to-Distal Energy Transfer in the Golf Swing"
subtitle: "Mechanisms, Evidence, and Counterfactual Tests of Distal-Handoff Timing"
author:
  - name: "Dieter Olson"
    affiliations:
      - name: "Independent Open Research"
date: "2026-08-08"
abstract: |
  Proximal-to-distal sequencing is commonly treated as evidence that mechanical
  energy should be transferred outward as early and completely as possible.
  This monograph tests a narrower proposition: transfer timing and sign depend
  on system state, geometry, contact constraints, and the counterfactual used.
  Reproducible planar, compliant-shaft, moving-base, two-hand, spatial, and
  reduced full-body models separate control, momentum, gravity, damping,
  elasticity, and contact contributions. Registered timing sweeps, same-state
  killswitches, work--energy balances, geometry reversals, cross-engine checks,
  and adverse-load controls identify mechanisms that are possible in the
  declared models and conditions that reverse or erase their effects.

  The results reject universal prescriptions. Delayed distal actuation can
  improve delivery in selected double-pendulum programs, separated hand forces
  can generate a negative late-downswing club couple without direct club torque,
  and passive structural pathways can alter delivery; however, matching rules
  materially change conclusions, elastic and proximal-rate effects retain both
  signs, and several observables are structurally non-identifying. An exact
  double-pendulum audit further shows that a fully excited seven-coefficient
  inverse model still cannot uniquely recover its declared eleven physical
  parameters. Model outputs therefore do not establish muscle action, intent,
  coaching strategy, anatomical validity, or equipment calibration.

  The release links each claim to equations, code, machine-readable results, and
  declared falsifiers. Independent human confirmation remains open because no
  governed participant dataset with synchronized bilateral six-axis grip
  wrenches, whole-body kinematics, ground reaction, club motion, and launch
  outcomes is currently available. The contribution is an open, testable
  framework for distinguishing feasible mechanisms from validated human effects.
keywords:
